*Reliable Measurement of Teachers' Instructional Practices with LLM Classifiers*

## Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to score teachers' instructional practices from classroom transcripts. Most validation studies focus on whether LLMs accurately classify individual utterances, but this does not establish whether scores created by aggregating those classifications are reliable across lessons. We extend generalizability theory to LLM-based scoring systems to examine the reliability of teacher-level scores produced by fixed model–prompt configurations. Unlike human raters, a fixed LLM classifier applies the same scoring rule each time it is used. However, classifier performance may vary systematically across teachers, creating errors that persist across their lessons. These systematic errors can appear as differences in teachers' instructional practice when they are instead artifacts of the classifier. Because these artifacts are reproducible, conventional reliability estimates may treat them as stable between-teacher differences and overstate how much reliable score variation reflects the intended construct. We develop a new reliability coefficient, construct-relevant reliability (CRR), which estimates the proportion of observed teacher-score variance that is both reproducible across lessons and attributable to true differences in instructional practice. CRR can be projected for different numbers and lengths of lessons using a relatively small human-coded validation sample. Monte Carlo simulations examine how classifier accuracy, systematic scoring differences, and study design jointly affect CRR. We then use CRR to compare 240 model–prompt configurations for measuring open-ended questioning in elementary science classrooms. Across simulations and the empirical application, results show that utterance-level accuracy alone is insufficient for selecting LLM-based scoring systems: configurations with similar classification performance can differ meaningfully in the reliability and validity of the teacher-level scores they produce.
